title: Email Etiquette
intro: The right opening and closing for the right relationship — a friend, a boss, a stranger. Get it wrong and the whole email reads off.

A2.right: your mother — a warm, everyday opening
A2.why: Family gets “Hi” plus the name: simple and warm.

A2.right: a stranger — very formal, name unknown
A2.why: When you don't know who will read it, this is the safe formal choice.

A2.right: a close friend — very casual opening
A2.why: Very relaxed: keep it for good friends.

A2.right: family, a partner or a close friend — a closing with affection
A2.why: “Love” before your name is for people close to your heart.

A2.right: a group of classmates — friendly opening for many people
A2.why: “Everyone” tells the reader the email goes to a whole group.

A2.right: a man you don't know well — formal opening with Mr
A2.why: Formal opening for a new contact: Dear + Mr + surname.

A2.right: a friend — casual closing about meeting again
A2.why: You expect to see them soon, so it's friendly and relaxed.

A2.right: a boss or client — polite professional closing
A2.why: The most common safe closing in British work emails.

A2.right: a doctor — formal opening with a professional title
A2.why: Use the title they earned: Dr, not Mr or Mrs.

A2.right: someone who helped you — simple, polite thanks
A2.why: Clear and polite: works for a shop, a hotel or a neighbour.

A2.right: a friend on their special day — cheerful opening
A2.why: Start with the reason you're writing: their birthday.

A2.left: Sorry, I can't come on Saturday.
A2.right: a friend's invitation — saying no politely
A2.why: Start with “Sorry” so the “no” sounds kind.

B1.right: a job application — formal opening addressed to the person hiring
B1.why: No name? Address the role: the person who will hire you.

B1.right: a group of colleagues — friendly opening to everyone
B1.why: Friendly and inclusive for people you work with every day.

B1.right: a friend or familiar colleague — warm casual opening
B1.why: The informal cousin of “I hope this email finds you well”.

B1.right: a formal contact you named at the start — professional closing
B1.why: You wrote “Dear Mr García”? Then finish with “Yours sincerely”.

B1.right: a friendly colleague — casual British closing that also means thanks
B1.why: Very common in British offices between people who get on; it means both “thanks” and “bye”.

B1.right: an official document for any reader — very formal, a bit old-fashioned
B1.why: Used for references and notices that anyone might read.

B1.right: a friend you'll phone shortly — casual closing
B1.why: “Speak” suggests a call or chat is coming.

B1.right: a client you know well — friendly professional closing
B1.why: “Warm” adds a touch of friendship to “regards”.

B1.left: Thank you for your quick reply.
B1.right: a business that answered fast — polite opening thanks
B1.why: Thanking them first sets a positive tone.

B1.right: a colleague who is leaving work for good — warm opening
B1.why: Retirement is a big moment: open with the good wishes.

B1.left: I am writing to complain about...
B1.right: a company that gave bad service — formal opening for a complaint
B1.why: State the purpose straight away, calmly and formally.

B1.right: a friend you forgot to answer — casual apology
B1.why: With an exclamation mark it's light and friendly, not formal.

B2.right: a university tutor — formal opening with title
B2.why: Academic staff get their title: Professor or Dr.

B2.right: a friend or friendly colleague — very casual, chatty British opening
B2.why: Very British and very casual: fine with friends and friendly colleagues, never in a formal email.

B2.left: I hope this message finds you well.
B2.right: a professional contact — formal, slightly old-fashioned opening
B2.why: A polite first line; some people now find it a bit stiff.

B2.right: a friend who is ill — warm, caring closing
B2.why: You hope they recover quickly: kind and personal.

B2.right: an unnamed formal recipient — closing when you don't know their name
almost anyone — a friendly, safe closing
B2.why: Friendly but neutral: fine for nearly any reader.

B2.right: a colleague who hasn't replied — gentle, casual follow-up
B2.why: A light nudge without sounding impatient.

B2.right: a colleague or client — brief, appreciative closing
B2.why: Shorter than “Thank you very much”, still professional.

B2.right: a new colleague on their first day — friendly opening
B2.why: From ships: you've joined the crew.

B2.left: Please accept my apologies for the delay.
B2.right: a client waiting for your answer — formal apology
B2.why: Formal, full apology for keeping a client waiting.

B2.right: a large group, some you don't know — neutral opening
B2.why: Neutral and efficient for mailing lists and big groups.

B2.right: someone you've just asked a favour — closing before they help
B2.why: You thank them before they act; use it with care, it can sound pushy.

C1.left: I am writing on behalf of the board.
C1.right: a formal representative context — professional, authoritative opening
C1.why: You speak for the board, not just yourself.

C1.right: a friend who has just written to you — warm reply opening
C1.why: You're replying with pleasure to their message.

C1.right: a formal complaint or error context — professional, remorseful
C1.why: “Sincere” makes the apology serious and formal.

C1.left: I would be happy to provide any further information.
C1.right: a client you are serving — offering further help, formally
C1.why: The natural British way to offer more help; avoid the Spanish-style “I remain at your disposal”.

C1.left: Do give my regards to the family.
C1.right: a family friend — warm, polite closing

C1.left: I look forward to your prompt response.
C1.right: a formal business contact — professional closing with urgency
C1.why: “Prompt” politely says: please don't take long.

C1.right: a close friend — casual, informal closing
C1.why: A friendly question suggesting you meet or chat.

C1.left: Looking forward to working with you.
C1.right: a new business partner — closing that welcomes the work ahead
C1.why: A natural British closing line when a project or partnership is just starting: warm but professional.

C1.right: an email sent by accident — asking them to ignore it
a friend with good career news — cheerful opening
C1.why: “Congrats” is the casual short form of “congratulations”.

C1.left: I should be most grateful for your assistance.
C1.right: a formal request — highly polite, very British
a colleague you work with closely — one-word ask for opinions
C1.why: One word inviting comments; only for close colleagues.
